newsitem.title: FRANCE: French mediator to legalise thousands of immigrants.
newsitem.headline: French mediator to legalise thousands of immigrants.

text.p: French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, keeping an election campaign promise, appointed a mediator on Tuesday to grant residence permits to thousands of illegal immigrants on terms set by a civil rights watchdog.

Jospin's office said Jean-Michel Galabert, a judge at the Council of State, the country's top administrative court, would oversee a case-by-case examination of tens of thousands of applications for legalisation, mostly from Africans.
Government officials across the country would be instructed to legalise immigrants fulfilling at least one of six criteria set by the National Consultative Council on Human Rights.

After meeting leaders of those campaigning for legal residence papers, Jospin adviser Jacques Rigaudiat told reporters: "We explained that pending the abrogation of the (immigration) laws, the criteria established by the human rights commission for examining individual cases would be applied."

Those who will get residency include parents of children born in France, spouses of immigrants with legal status, those in danger if sent home, patients receiving intensive medical care, students and immigrants "well-integrated in French society".

The move seemed bound to raise an outcry on the right. Opinion polls show most voters want the hardline legislation enacted by former right-wing interior ministers Charles Pasqua and Jean-Louis Debre to stay.

Rigaudiat and two other senior officials met a delegation of "sans papiers" ("without papers") protesters who marched to Paris from the southwestern city of Angouleme to request residence permits refused by the previous conservative government.
Many of them are Malians who have lived in France for years. They say they were deprived of residence rights by a stiffening of immigration laws in 1993.

The left, which won a parliamentary election 10 days ago, has vowed to repeal laws it says violate France's tradition of hospitality and pander to the extreme-right National Front, which wants to send some three million immigrants home.

The exact number of immigrants who could win residence rights under the review ordered by Jospin was unclear. The daily Le Monde put it at 20,000 to 40,000. A spokesman for the protesters said it could affect 100,000.
The issue sparked nationwide controversy last August when police stormed a Paris church and forcibly evicted some 200 Africans who had taken refuge there to avoid expulsion.
Magistrates later overturned orders expelling most of them.
Many "sans papiers" are in a legal limbo. They can neither obtain residence rights nor be expelled for a variety of reasons -- including having children born in France.
Earlier this year, Debre pushed through a law intended to close legal loopholes, drawing protests by film-makers and academics for further clamping down on immigration.
There are an estimated five million foreigners in France, of whom about one million, mostly North Africans, are thought to be illegal.
